4. As per this approved plan the appellant proceeded very far in its implementation; it purchased 65 bighas of land, got into possession of another 150 bighas by agreements with the owners, prepared and allotted 250 plots and made commitment for allotment of 413 plots to different members of the public. Then the DIT suddenly made a proposal on 16 September 1987 to the Government for acquiring 390 bighas of land including the entire 300 bighas area of the appellant's Lay-out Plan whereupon LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 started under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 (Ordinance No. 2 of 1982). Having got this information the appellant raised objection to the DIT's Chairman, met him on several occasions and requested him to exclude its land from the proposed Acquisition proceedings but to no effect. Neither the DIT nor the Land Acquiring Authority served any notice upon the appellant though the appellant had been in possession of a major part of the land since 1983. In these circumstances, the appellant made a representation to the President who thereupon called for a report. Report came and it is dated 12 November 1989 (Annexure-D) signed by the DIT's Chairman. In this report the Chairman admitted that the land proposed by DIT for acquisition was already included in the appellant's Lay-out Plan and that this land should have been excluded from his proposal dated 16 September 1987. On perusal of the report the Government-in the Ministry of Public Works, which is the DIT's Controlling Authority-by an order dated 27 January 1990 (Annexure-E) directed that the land covered by the Appellant's Lay-out Plan be excluded from acquisition. Copies of this order were forwarded to all concerned including the appellant and it was further directed that necessary action be taken as per this order. But seven months after, the same Ministry issued an order dated 13 August 1990 (Annexure-H) cancelling the order dated 27 January 1990 (Annexure-E); by two subsequent orders, one dated 6.9.90 and the other dated 27.9.90 (Annexures H1 and H2), this Ministry partially modified the order in Annexure 'H' exempting thereby only 62 bighas (more or less) of land from the proposed acquisition under LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88. This exclusion, the appellant contends, will not serve any purpose and this, along with the acquisition of land for widening the Ranabhola Road will sabotage the entire Housing Project. In this background the applicability of the doctrine of promissory estoppel is to be considered. 

 5. The principle of promissory estoppel is now well established in the Administrative Law. It has been evolved by Courts on the basis of 'equity' to avoid gross injustice particularly when the injustice results from strict application of any rule or procedure of law. This principle applies to a case where a promise is made by one person to another, relying on which the promise has materially altered his position, but subsequently the promissor tries to back out. It may be defined as: where one party by words or conduct has made a clear and definite promise which he knows will be acted upon by the promisee and the latter, in fact, has acted upon it, then the promise is binding upon its maker who will not be entitled to back up on it. This principle of promissory estoppel is available by way of defence and also as a cause of action. This principle is applicable against the government and a statutory body as well as against a private individual. In the case of government or a public authority, mere "executive necessity" or "change of policy" is not available as a defence if the promisee has already altered this position by acting upon the promise. The learned Additional Attorney-General has contended that the principle of promissory estoppel is not available to prevent the Government from discharging its statutory function. By this he wants to say that acquisition of land for a public purpose is made by the Government under Ordinance No. 11 of 1982 and that in this case, if this principle is applied the Government will be prevented from discharging their statutory functions. We do not think that exclusion of the appellant's land from the area covered by the Land Acquisition Proceeding will stand in the way of the Government from discharging its statutory functions. The correct position of law is that by applying this doctrine the Government or for that purpose any person cannot be compelled to do something which is prohibited by law or that the promissory estoppel cannot prevent a legislative body from making a law. However, if the Government or a public authority is bound to keep its promise, it will not be so bound when a greater public interest requires that the promise should not be acted upon. Similarly, the promissory estoppel is not available in the case of vital change of circumstances that takes place subsequent to the making of the promise. Again, when public interests clash with private interests, it is the former which will get the priority. In this case, however, we find no such clash of interests, for the purpose of the acquisition of land under the LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 is the same as the purpose of the appellant's Lay-out Plan which is already implemented to a great extent, i.e. developing the land for construction of residential buildings. But what is a greater public interest cannot be left to be decided by the Government alone, but it must be scrutinized by the Court on the basis of materials produced before it. A "greater public interest" cannot be treated as a guarded secret; it must be disclosed. Of course, if the promise has been made by an officer of the government (or a statutory body) who got no power or authority to do so, then the promise is not binding upon the government. Again, when the government or any public authority thinks that the promise cannot be implemented in the greater public interest or for any latches on the part of the promisee, it must give the promisee a reasonable notice or opportunity to rectify the latches. In this case no notice was given; on the contrary, the broad fact that the land proposed by RAJUK for acquisition was already included in the appellant's housing project, approved by RAJUK itself long ago, has been suppressed in the Acquisition proposal. Again, seven months after the issuing of the rectification order (Annexure-E), the Government, obviously at the instance of the RAJUK, raised, for the first time, the question of the appellant's title to the land. This is a lame excuse, for in the case of a Lay-out Plan under the Town Improvement Act, 1953 prior acquisition of title is not necessary. Nor prior acquisition of title was a condition attached to the Layout Plan. Title is necessary for actual construction of a building under the Building Construction Act, 1952. Another instance of bad faith of the RAJUK is that in the Lay-out Plan there is a condition that the appellant will have no objection to "future acquisition of land for construction of bridges or culverts and their approaches to Ranibhola Road". This condition does not include extension of the Ranibhola Road itself. This road was already there, 100 ft. wide. But to widen this road to 300 ft., petitioner's land was proposed to be acquired under LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87; furthermore, in that connection, the Lay-out Plan was sought to be re-aligned in such a way as to spoil the entire scheme. These acts and conduct of the RAJUK unerringly indicate something mala fide. In view of the facts and circumstances in particular, the conduct of the DIT, now RAJUK, the proposed acquisition, practically of the whole of the appellant's land under the Lay-out Plan, is not just and fair. It is not found to have been made in the larger public-interest so as to overcome the bar of the doctrine of promissory estoppel. The doctrine of promissory estoppel is, as I find, applicable to this case with all its force. The impugned orders in Annexures-H, H(1) and H(2) are therefore invalid; the order in Annexure-E stands. 

 7. On 4 October 1978 the Board of Trustees of respondent No. 2 Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakhya, gave no objection to the appellant's proposed housing project on condition that the project would be built on lands in the appellant's own possession. On 29 February 1983 when the layout plan was approved one further condition was added namely, that the appellant would have no objection to further acquisition of land by respondent No. 2 for construction of bridge or culverts and their approaches to Ranabhola for extension of Uttara scheme of respondent No.2. When a part of the land included in the appellant's lay-out plan was acquired in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 for the Uttara Ranabola link road the appellant did not challenge that acquisition under the Acquisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982) When the acquisition proceeding in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 for extension of Uttara Township was nearing completion the appellant made a representation to the President on 2 October, 1989. The Ministry of Works, respondent No. 1, gave a decision on 27 January 1990 to the effect that the area of land for which respondent No. 2 had given no objection be excluded from acquisition. A few months later on 13 August 1990 that order was cancelled, but a memorandum was issued on 6 September 1990 asking all authorities to keep those lands of the appellant for which it submitted documents of title out of acquisition. Finally, on 27 September 1990 only 21.09 acres of land of the appellant was kept out of acquisition. This was the end result of the appellant's representations made by the appellant bypassing the channel of objection provided in Ordinance No. II of 1982. The "no objection" of respondent No. 2 to the proposed housing project or the approval of the lay-out plan of that project can hardly be a basis of promissory estoppel with regard to those lands for which the appellant failed to produce any document of title or ownership. No objection or approval to a speculative venture of a land developer having no possession in the land of the proposed venture would not be an authorized act under the Town Improvement Act, 1953. Respondent No. 2, a statutory body entrusted with the development, improvement and expansion of the Capital of the Republic and its environs, could not, and it did not, give no objection to the appellant for building a housing project on lands belonging to others. 

 The appellant's representation cannot be construed to be one under section 52 of the Town Improvement Act, 1953, which provided for alternation of any improvement scheme or housing scheme where proviso (a), (b) or (c) is attracted. It was never the case of the appellant that any of the provisos in section 52 is attracted in its case. The acquisition of land in this case was clearly for a public purpose. There ought not to have been any interference in the matter. 

 9. The appellant, a private limited company, is engaged, inter alia, in the business of undertaking housing projects. It is not disputed that respondent No. 2 Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha, briefly, RAJUK, (previously DIT) is a statutory authority, inter alia, to frame and execute improvement schemes to provide housing accommodation if it is found expedient and for the public advantage under the Town Improvement Act, 1953 (EB Act XIII of 1953), briefly, the Act. At the instance of RAJUK lands were acquired in two LA cases, Nos. 4 of 1986-87 and 2 of 1987-88 in mouza Bailjuri, PS Uttara, first for a connecting road from Uttara Model Town to Ranabhola and secondly, for extension of the Uttara Model Town itself (393.00 acres in the second case) under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982) briefly the Ordinance. The appellant had a private housing project in the same area under the name "MOHUA", said to be comprising of 300 bighas, which was undertaken with the approval of the then DIT given in 1978. The said land allegedly belonging to the appellant having also been acquired in the aforesaid two LA cases, there ensued a clash of interest between the appellant and the RAJUK which provides the background of the appellant's writ petition. 

 10. I shall come back to the facts of the case fully and in a formal manner as set out by the parties in their petitions and affidavits before the High Court Division. But I would like to mention here at the first chance the most important fact of the case and that is, the appellant never raised any objection to the aforesaid acquisitions under the provisions of the Ordinance and RAJUK have already paid more than Taka 92 crore towards compensation in 1989 following final decision by the Government before the filing of the writ petition in 1991. The acquisition proceedings have not been questioned even in the writ petition. The appellant filed the writ petition challenging certain Government orders which followed a representation by the appellant to the President on 2.10.89 regarding acquisition of its alleged land. I do not find any provision in the Ordinance or any law under which a party aggrieved by an acquisition proceeding can approach the President of the country for redress. The remedy is provided in the Ordinance itself. If a person is allowed to bypass the Ordinance and take his grievance directly to the Head of the State, it will not only amount to a no-confidence in the rule of law but also encourage very positively the expedient way of, what is called, "access" or "tadbir". It is particularly disturbing for the judicial conscience because it is unthinkable that a person can be permitted to come up with a petition of complaint directly to the Chief Justice when the law of the land requires him to go to a Magistrate. All the Government orders in this case, I am constrained to observe, are, therefore not at all in accordance with law, particularly when the Government have already decided about the acquisition finally under section 5 of the Ordinance. There is no power reserved in the Government to revise its decision of acquisition under the Ordinance. The LA cases being undoubtedly for a public purpose and the appellant not having availed of the remedy under the Ordinance and not having ever challenged the acquisition proceeding either in the present writ petition or at any time before any court, I am of the view that no injustice has been done to it by discharging the rule in the writ petition. 

 12. The appellant's case, briefly, is that in order to establish and develop a housing project under the name "MOHUA" it selected a part of mouza Bailjuri and applied to the Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) for approval of the said housing project. The Board of Trustees of the DIT in its meeting held on 4.10.1978 approved the project and authorized the Town Planner to approve the layout plan of the project; after several exchanges between the appellant-company and the DIT and modification of the layout plan by the company, the DIT approved the company's layout plan comprising more or less 300 bighas of land of 99 CS plots as a whole and part of 17 CS plots by memo dated 27.2.83. Upon receipt of the clearance as to the layout plan of the company's housing project the company started development of the land by cutting, filling and levelling earth and demarcating plots and road, spending a lot of capital. The company purchased by registered instrument more or less 45 bighas of land out of the said 300 bighas and also took possession by right of contract for purchase of another 150 bighas of land of the layout plan. The company allotted 130 plots to intending purchasers and committed allotment of another 413 plots to the public. Another 140 plots had been allotted to the persons who entered into contract for sale of their land to the company. When the company was deeply in the midst of executing their housing project according to the layout plan, it was learnt that a move was taken by the DIT to change the width of alignment of the Ranabhola Link Road which would seriously affect the project of the company, spoiling 60 developed plots and 107 allotted plots. The DIT, now RAJUK, proposed to acquire land for the said link road (as per deviation) under LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87; the company moved the authorities against the said deviation but ultimately RAJUK did not do anything; on the contrary, RAJUK proposed to the Government for acquisition of land of Bailjuri Mouza for extension of RAJUK's Uttara Township housing project within which the land of the approved layout plan of the company had also been included. This acquisition proposal was approved by the Government and proceeding was being taken for acquisition in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88. 

 Failing to obtain redress of its grievances against RAJUK's malafide and unjust acts of deviation of road plan and acquisition of land from within the layout plan the appellant filed a petition to the President of Bangladesh on 2.10.89 and RAJUK through its Chairman, submitted a detailed report on 12.11.89 to the Ministry of Works (which is the administrative Ministry of RAJUK) and addressed a copy of the said report to the President's Secretariat; the Government at its highest level decided on 27.1.90 (Annexure E to the writ petition) that the area over which clearance had been given by the RAJUK to the appellant is to be left out of acquisition for RAJUK's project and directed to issue necessary order to all concerned immediately. 

 13. The then Chairman of RAJUK Mr. Rahmatullah (respondent No. 3) and some officials of RAJUK were ill-disposed to the appellant and its success in the field of housing project and being determined to see the project spoiled totally, started manoeuvering against the appellant's interest and having found in the new Secretary-in-charge of the Ministry of Works, Mr. MA Rouf an ally (respondent No. 4) who had been an officer subordinate to Mr. Rahmatullah in the Public Works Department, RAJUK tried to re-open the settled issue and through Mr. Rouf had an order issued on 13.8.90 cancelling the Government decision dated 27.1.90. This order dated 13.8.1990 is Annexure H to the Writ petition. The appellant again petitioned the President of Bangladesh against that order on 5.9.1990 and while such appeal petition was pending, another order was passed by memo dated 6.9.90 purporting to modify the order contained in Memo dated 13.8.90. This new order proposed to keep small portion of the lands of the original layout plan of the appellant outside the acquisition for RAJUK. Again, after few days another order was issued by Memo dated 27.9.90 purporting to modify the order contained in the earlier Memo dated 6.9.90 reducing the quantum of land to be kept out of acquisition for RAJUK. These two orders dated 6.9.90 and 27.9.90 are Annexures H (1) and H (2) to the writ petition. The appeal to the President was not disposed of due to political situation in the country and subsequent change of the Government and the holding of general election to Parliament. 

 15. Respondents No. 1 and 2 filed separate affidavits-in-opposition but taking similar lines. They denied the allegations of the appellant. They have also challenged the allegation that by huge expenditure of money the appellant developed the aforesaid area for selling up the alleged housing project. The contesting respondents, however, admitted that respondent No. 2 approved a layout plan submitted by the appellant on certain conditions which were required to be fulfilled by the appellant. Subsequently, it transpired that the appellant did not fulfill these conditions. It was found that the appellant did not develop the land as proposed by it for selling up the housing project. Subsequently, the RAJUK decided to extend its Uttara Housing Project for developing more residential plots and, as such, it proposed for acquisition of 393 acres of land which included the land as per layout plan of the appellant. It transpired that the appellant had no title in the land included in its layout plan and the appellant could not produce any paper in order to establish its title therein. In pursuance of the proposal of RAJUK to construct the Ranabhola link road and to extend the Uttara Housing Project the Government decided to acquire land under section 4 of the Ordinance, and accordingly, after undergoing all necessary procedures required for acquisition of land under the said Ordinance and after payment of necessary I compensation to the real owners of the land, acquired the same in LA Case Nos. 4 of 1986-7 and 2 of 1987-88. Even if the appellant had any interest in any portion of the acquired land, after the order of acquisition, this land vested in the Government and the appellant is only entitled to receive compensation thereof and cannot claim any other interest therein. 

 17. It appears from the impugned judgment that the Rule was pressed on three grounds-1) that having once approved that layout plan submitted by the appellant RAJUK cannot go back on its approval and propose acquisition of the disputed land to the detriment and interest of the appellant on the principle of promissory estoppel, 2) that the impugned orders were violative of Articles 40 and 42 of the Constitution and 3) that the purpose for which the land had been acquired being similar to the purpose pursued by the appellant it could not be deemed to be a public purpose. 

 20. Although leave was granted to examine all the finding of the High Court Division, Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellant, submitted that there are only two main points to be considered in the appeal. Later on however, Mr. Ahmed raised some other points which will be noticed in due course. Mr. Ahmed's first and main submission is based on the doctrine of promissory estoppel for which he relied on the cases of MP Sugar Mills Vs. State of UP and VR Vora Vs. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay AIR 1979 (SC) 621 and AIR 1991 (SC) 14 respectively. Mr. Ahmed submits that the then DIT having approved the layout plan of the appellant for the housing project under section 74(3) of the Act and the appellant having acted on such approval, respondent No. 2 was precluded on the aforesaid principle of promissory estoppel to put forward any proposal for acquisition of the land included in the layout plan. The learned Additional Attorney-General for respondent No. 1 and the learned Advocate for RAJUK respondent No. 2 have submitted that the principle of promissory estoppel has no application in the case as there is no provision of approval either under section 74(3) or any section of the Act and, more importantly, the appellant, in any case, was never given a carte blanche in respect of the land included in the layout plan as claimed by it. The appellant was given a sort of no objection certificate subject to a clear condition that it can undertake its housing project only on the land in its possession. Since there is nothing to show that the appellant was in possession of 300 bighas of land when the layout plan was approved on 27.2.83, there was nothing to prevent respondent No. 2 for giving a proposal for acquisition of land for extension of the Uttara township which is its statutory duty. The learned Additional Attorney-General strenuously I argued that the appellant's plea of promissory estoppel will be of no avail now as it had not taken any objection in the LA Cases under the Ordinance and the Government have taken final decision long ago for acquisition under section 5 or the Ordinance and the lands vested in the Government under section 11 of the said Ordinance as the compensation money has been deposited by the Deputy Commissioner in the public account on 25.11.1989. He showed the relevant chalan to us. 

 In the writ petition there is no averment at all that on that date i.e. on 4.10.78 or even on 27.2.83 when the layout plan was approved "as per resolution of the Board of Trustees of DIT", the appellant was in possession of 300 bighas of land or any land as per its layout plan. There is no reference to the area of land even in the order dated 27.2.83. It is only in 1991 that the appellant stated in its writ petition long after 8 years that it purchased so far 45 bighas of land and had taken possession by right of contract for purchase of another about 150 bighas of land. There was, however, no document produced in support of its assertion. 

 26. It will be seen that the Government gave cogent reasons in its letter dated 10.8.1990 (Annexure-H) for cancelling its earlier order dated 27.1.1990 (Annexure-E) excluding the 300 bighas from acquisition. Annexure-H shows that it was made subordinating the private interest of the appellant to the greater interest of the public. In this connection the learned Additional Attorney-General submitted that the plea of promissory estoppel is not available against the Government in the facts of the present case and he drew inspiration for the purpose from MP Sugar Mills Case, AIR 1979 (SC) 621, which, inter alia says: 

 27. To determine which way the equity lies in this case, I shall refer to only one of the facts for which the Government cancelled its earlier order dated 27.1.1990. Admittedly, a large part of the land included in the appellant's layout plan was acquired in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 for the Ranabhola link road and the appellant raised no objection under the Ordinance except making two representations to the Chairman DIT. According to the appellant, the said acquisition had the effect of damaging its project spoiling 60 developed and 137 allotted plots. In 1986 the DIT had taken up the work of construction of the link road from Uttara to Ranabhola, vide appellant's own admission in its letter dated 17.11.86 to the Chairman, DIT (Annexure-C). The Appellant could not lawfully object to the said acquisition because there was a condition that it would not object to future acquisition of land by DIT for construction of bridges or culverts and their approaches to Ranabhola for extension of Uttara scheme (Vide Annexure B). The appellant, therefore, lay low at that time and without raising any objection under the Ordinance against the said acquisition or the subsequent acquisition or without going to Court started moving the corridors of power which was apparently found convenient and pursued to the last until the table turned in December, 1990. The President was first moved when the acquisition proceeding in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 for extension of Uttara Township was almost coming to a close. 

 28. Now the effect of the order dated 27.1.1990 was that the entire 300 bighas claimed by the appellant was to be excluded from acquisition. Was it physically possible when an unknown urea out of the said 300 bighas was already consumed admittedly by a 300-ft wide public road? This is one or the many reasons why the impugned order was passed cancelling the earlier order. This is a good reason for which private interest must yield to public interest. There was no scope for the High Court Division to interfere with the impugned orders because in case the Rule was made absolute, the order dated 27.1.90 would revive and the effect would be to ignore the reality of an already existing public road. 

 "I. Because in view of the provisions of Part III (Sections 38 to 51 A) and section 79 of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and the fact that the respondents have not pleaded sanction or notification of sanction in either of the two cases of acquisition (LA Case No. 4/86-87 and LA Case No. 2/87-88) the alleged acquisition proceedings are all without lawful authority and no vesting has taken place as urged on behalf of the respondents. 

 II. Because in view of the provisions of section 79 of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and section 15 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and the fact that the respondents have not pleaded or proved any agreement required to be entered into under section 15(1) of the Ordinance which is a mandatory provision, the acquisition proceeding in the two LA cases are without lawful authority and no vesting of the lands in question had taken place as submitted by the respondents." 

 The appellant cannot be permitted to assail the acquisition proceedings raising new grounds on facts at this stage, particularly because there was no challenge in the writ petition regarding the said proceedings. The grounds are not only beyond the leave order but beyond the writ petition also. However, in order to meet the aforesaid grounds the respondents have supplied copies of letters showing respondent No. 2's proposal for acquisition of 393 acres of land for extension of Uttara Township and Government’s sanction for the said acquisition. A copy of the agreement dated 10 June 1988 in connection with LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 as required under section 15 of the Ordinance has also been supplied. From these papers it appears that there was no procedural illegality in the acquisition proceeding. 

 31. It is on record that the land shown in the layout plan of the appellant was included in the original Uttara township project. The Central Land Allocation Committee allotted 3300.00 acres of land in 1960 for the project. But the DIT because of financial constraint acquired only 951.00 acres before. It is evident that the acquisition of 393 acres in LA Cases No. 2 of 1987-88 was for the same purpose and it is incongruous that a small area inside the big public project will be in private hands doing the same job. Of necessity, the public facilities like, roads, bridges, schools, parks, etc. will be provided in the public project and the private entrepreneur will have the benefit of those facilities without making any investment in that behalf at all. From H and H1 it appears that the appellant and the Capital Housing Society have been allowed to retain 21.09 acres of land on the basis of documents produced by them subject to verification. They will thus be able to make allotments of their own lands without taking any responsibility for the public facilities as are required to be provided in a housing project. For example, the Ranabhola link road which runs across the appellant's layout plan lands was constructed by the respondent but the benefit of the same will be squarely drawn by the private allottees of the appellant. Considering the public interest and the contents of the impugned orders by which the appellant has not been wholly deprived and at least it has been allowed to retain those lands for which it has been able to produce documents, it appears that substantial justice has been done to it. 

 35. The appellant filed the writ petition calling into question three Orders passed by respondent No. 1 Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development dated 13.8.90 (Annexure-H), 6.9.90 (Annexure-H1) and 27.9.90 (Annexure-H2) relating to acquisition of land in LA Case No.4 of 1986-87 and LA Case No.2 of 1987-88. The appellant is a Private Limited Company incorporated on 3.6.75 for the purpose, inter alia, of acquiring land, constructing houses and buildings, dealing with and improving property, undertaking housing projects, transacting business of real estate agent, etc. The appellant selected an area of about 300 bighas of land at Mouza Biljuri, JL No. 201, under PS Uttara and prepared a housing project named "Mahua". It submitted an application on 28.3.78 to the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (now Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha), shortly the Kartripakkha, respondent No. 2, for a no objection certificate. It wanted to develop the area as a housing project in association with the owners of the land with a view to selling plots of land therefrom to intending purchasers among the members of the public. The Board of Trustees of respondent No. 2, the highest decision-making body of the Kartripakkha, in its meeting held on 4.10.78 (Annexure-A) approved of the said project in the following terms: 

 2, That you will have no objection to future acquisition of land by DIT for construction of bridge or culverts and their approaches to Ranabhola for extension of Uttara Scheme of DIT. 

 37. The layout plan shows a 100 feet wide road from Uttara to Ranabhola to be built in future by the Kartripakkha the width and alignment of which were inserted in the layout plan in apparent consultation with the agreement of the Kartipakkha. The appellant thereafter started survey, clearance of trees and shrubs, earth cutting, earth filling, levelling, demarcating and plotting in phases at huge expenses as the area consisted generally of low and marshy land. The appellant claims to have purchased so far by registered deeds 65 bighas of land more or less and has claimed to have taken possession of another 150 big has of land by entering into contracts of purchase with the owners. It has already allotted 250 plots and committed allotment of another 413 plots to the members of the public. The Kartripakkha has sanctioned house building plans on several plots of land allotted by the appellant. While in the midst of developing the housing project the appellant was surprised to learn that respondent No. 2 proposed to acquire land for the said Uttara-Ranabhola link road the width of which had been increased to 300 feet without informing and consulting the appellant and had changed the road alignment piercing through the heart of the appellant's housing project. The said deviation will spoil 60 developed and 137 allotted plots of the appellant. It submitted a detailed representation to the Chairman of the Kartripakkha by a letter dated 17.11.86 (Annexures-C and C 1) objecting to the proposed deviation, with no answer. The Managing Director of the appellant met the Chairman of respondent No. 2 and following the meeting sent him another letter dated 17.6.87 requesting him to cancel the proposed disastrous deviation from the approved layout plan and the Chairman promised to do so, but the Kartripakkha, on the contrary, proposed to the Government to acquire land of Bailjuri Mouza for extension of their Uttara Housing Project wherein the entire lands of approved layout plan of the appellant had also been included. The Kartripakkha got their proposal for acquisition approved by the Government and proceeded with the acquisition of land in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88. The appellant approached the President on 2.10.89 for redress of its grievances and also sent a detailed representation dated 30.10.89 to the Secretary, Ministry or Land Administration and Land Reforms to keep the appellant's housing project out of the Kartripakkha's acquisition. Upon receipt of the President's remark on the appellant's application the Ministry of Works, respondent No.1, asked for a detailed report on the matter from the Chairman of the Kartripakkha who sent a report on 12.11.89 (Annexure-D) to the Ministry stating, inter alia, that for the establishment of Uttara Model Town the former Dhaka Improvement Trust obtained an allotment of 3,300 acres of land in 1960 from the Central Land Allocation Committee, but for paucity of fund only 951 acres were acquired initially. Taking into account the pressing problem of housing the former Trust requested the Government to acquire a further area of 393.00 acres of land of Bailjuri Mouza by Memo dated 16.9.87. The Ministry of Works and the Ministry of Land approved or the proposal on 29.12.87 and 4.5.88 respectively. It was further stated in the report that at the time of making the proposal on 16.9.87 the former Trust should have left out 200 bighas of land for which the appellant had an approved layout plan. After receiving the said report the Ministry of Works, respondent No.1, by a Memo dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E) gave a decision that the area for which clearance has been given by the Kartripakkha to the appellant by their letter dated 27.2.83 (Annexure-B) is to be left out of acquisition and requested to issue necessary orders immediately to all concerned including the Ministry of Land, the acquiring authority. A copy of this Memo dated 27.1.90 was also forwarded to the appellant. The Memo contains a map and plot index to be excluded from acquisition. 

 38. It is the appellant's case that the then Chairman of the Kartripakkha and some Officials of the Ministry of Works who were not well-disposed towards' the appellant were determined to spoil its housing project and by asking the appellant to submit the deeds of all the lands purchased by it to prove Its ownership of lands diverted the real issue. Even then the appellant submitted details of its purchased lands and lands in possession by letter dated 20.6.90. The appellant addressed several letters to give effect to Annexure-E and after some inconclusive meetings with the appellant, respondent No. 1 suddenly issued the first impugned Memo dated 13.8.90 (Annexure-H) purporting to cancel the order dated 27.1.90 (Annexure E) and requesting all authorities to keep out of acquisition only those lands of the appellants, over which the appellants acquired full title to the complete satisfaction of the authority and also which will be found to have contained 3 or more acres in a block. There will be no re-opening of LA Case No. 4/86-87 for which land had already been acquired. Respondent No. 1 issued the second impugned Memo dated 6.9.90 Annexure H1, asking all authorities to keep out of acquisition those lands or the appellant for which it has submitted valid documents of title. The third impugned Memo was issued on 27.9.90 (Annexure H2) the ultimate outcome of which is that the entire LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 was kept intact keeping out of acquisition only 21.09 acres of land of the appellant, which, the appellant says, will entirely sabotage its housing project. 

 Both respondent No. 1 and respondent No. 2 filed separate affidavits-in-opposition, the first one stating that the appellant was given a no objection certificate "on its own possessed land" and the second one Slating that the project was approved "only on land owned" by the appellant and both of them commonly stating that the appellant did not fulfill the conditions on which the approval to its project and layout plan was given. In particular it was denied that the appellant improved any land. They also stated that at the time of "requisition" of land under the two LA Cases the appellant did not raise any objection with the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, under the provisions of Ordinance No. II of 1982. The appellant petitioned to respondent No. 1 only after acquisition of the land. The acquisition process under the two LA cases rightly proceeded and culminated in the payment of compensation to the owners of the land, except the appellant and, as such, the property now vests in the Government In spite of repeated requests the appellant failed to furnish its documents of title and papers showing mutation of any land in its favour. 

 41. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submission that the High Court Division erred in law in taking the view that the respondents changed their earlier decision for non-fulfillment of conditions on which the layout plan was approved, that is, the appellant did not acquire title to the land, that there was no such condition at all for the approval of the layout plan as well as for the exemption under Annexure-E. that for the development of housing projects prior acquisition of title to the land is not necessary, vide section 74(3) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 under which the appellant's layout plan was approved, that the High Court Division was confused as to the provisions of the Town Improvement Act and the Building Constructions Act; that the respondents took extraneous matters into consideration while changing their earlier decision and that the appellant's fundamental right to enter into and carry on any lawful trade and business under Article 40 of the Constitution has been infringed by the impugned orders. 

 42. I have no disagreement with the submissions of Mr. A W Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for respondent No.1 that if the acquisition of 393 acres of land is complete under section 11 of Ordinance No. II of 1982 then it is no use crying over the spilt milk and that the transaction is a past and closed one; but I do not agree upon the facts presented to us that acquisition is fait accompli in this case. Under section 11 of the Ordinance, the property shall stand acquired and vested absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances when the compensation mentioned in the award under section 7 has been paid or is deemed to have been paid in pursuance of section 10. Section 11 also provides that immediately after the acquisition of the property a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner in the prescribed form to that effect shall be published in the Official Gazelle. All that has been shown to us is a photocopy of a chalan in LA Case No. 2 of 1987 -88 dated 25.11.89 by which the Deputy Commissioner deposited a sum of Taka 92,61,36,586.77 in the public account for payment of compensation for acquisition of land in the said LA case. There has been a simple assertion in the affidavits-in-opposition of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 that the owners of the land, except the appellant, have since taken payment of the compensation, which the appellant stoutly denied in its affidavits-in-reply. Nothing else has been shown before the High Court Division or to us to induce any amount of assurance in our mind that after depositing the compensation money in the public account the Deputy Commissioner actually completed disbursement of the same among the owners. On the contrary it appears from Annexure G to the writ petition that several writ petitions have been filed in 1993 against the acquisition in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 by several owners which are still pending in the High Court Division and on perusal of the records of which I find that neither the Kartripakkha nor the Government have yet filed any affidavit-in-opposition to the same. The appellant has asserted that it has received no notice of acquisition in respect of any land under its ownership and possession and there has been no denial to this categorical assertion. How then is the acquisition a completed transaction? When we asked the learned Additional Attorney-General to produce the Gazette Notification under section 11 (2) of the Ordinance, he submitted that no Gazette Notification has yet been made. Not a single case of disbursement of compensation money has been brought to our notice. A photocopy of the Memo dated 16.9.87 by which the Kartripakkha requested respondent No.1 to acquire 393 acres of land of Mouza Bailjuri has been made available to/us by the learned Counsel for respondent No. 2. This Memo shows that the Central Land Allocation Committee allotted 3450 acres of land to the former Dhaka Improvement Trust for its Uttara Satellite Town Project in 1965, but for financial difficulties only 950 acres of land was decided to be acquired as a first block of the project. About the present stage of that project of 1965 it is stated in the said Memo that the acquisition of land for the said project is in its final stage. When that is the position with regard to the first block of Uttara Satellite Town Project, it is difficult for us to be assured by a mere statement in the affidavits-in-opposition that full compensation money has already been paid in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88. Besides, if the acquisition of 393 acres of land is complete, then how can respondent No. 1 pass the various impugned orders in Annexure-H series, making a freelance exercise of excluding some lands from acquisition, then again including it? Is this exercise a conclusive evidence of vesting of property in the Government? The learned Additional Attorney-General's argument is therefore thoroughly unacceptable to me. 

 43. True it is that the appellant has not challenged the acquisition proceedings in the two LA cases involved, but there is no denial to its assertion that it has not received any notice of acquisition in respect of lands under its ownership and possession and therefore its failure to challenge the acquisition proceeding, especially when the acquisition process is not yet complete, will not be fatal to it. The appellant's intention in filing the writ petition was to restore the order of respondent No. 1 dated 27.1.90 (Annexure E) and, with respect, I differ from my learned brother ATM Afzal J. that Annexure E has no legal basis and I will give my reasons later on. 

 44. The Town Improvement Act, 1953, shortly the Act, makes provisions for the development, improvement and expansion of the Capital of the Republic and Narayanganj and Tongi Municipalities and certain areas in their vicinity. The Kartripakkha is empowered under sections 38-42 to frame an improvement scheme or a rehousing scheme in respect of any area (which means that it is its discretion to frame or not to frame such a scheme) and after preparing a notice stating that a scheme has been framed and giving some particulars and the map of the area comprised in the scheme shall cause a notice to be published weekly for three consecutive weeks in the Official Gazette and in local newspapers and also send a copy of the notice to the Mayor of the Corporation or Chairman of the Pourashava under section 45. Thereafter within 30 days every person whose name appears in the Municipal Assessment List and the occupiers of the land have to be served with a notice under section 48. Considering any objection, representation and statement of dissent received thereunder and after hearing all persons making such objection, etc. the Kartripakkha may either abandon the scheme or apply to the Government for sanction of the scheme with or without modification under section 49 and the Government may sanction with or without modification or may refuse to sanction any improvement scheme under section 50. When the Government sanctions an improvement scheme it shall announce the fact by Notification and the publication of a Notification shall be conclusive evidence that the scheme has been duly framed and sanctioned under section 51. Similar provisions are there in section 51A in respect of schemes of Taka 5 lakh or more outside the City or Municipal limit. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the appellant, has additionally assailed the impugned orders on the ground that sections 38-51A of the said Act and section 15 of Ordinance No. II of 1982 have not been followed and I concur with my learned brother A TM Afzal, J. that these new allegations and grounds are not available to the appellant for the reasons given by him. 

 47. When a developer approaches the Kartripakkha for a no objection certificate with a scheme of its own it is absolutely not necessary that it should own any or all of the area covered by its plan. It approaches the Kartripakkha for an assurance that after the layout plan is approved it will be kept outside of any other developer's or the Kartripakkha's own improvement scheme or acquisition plan, subject of course to the fulfilment of conditions that the Kartripakkha may impose upon the approval. 

 50. Respondent No. 2 has not made any averment nor placed any material to show that before submitting its own scheme for acquisition on 16.9.87 any enquiry was made by the Kartripakkha as to how far the appellant had proceeded with its housing project. It did not cancel the appellant's approval and sanction before sending its own proposal for acquisition and hence reliance upon section 21 of the General Clauses Act by the High Court Division and its renewed plea by the learned Additional Attorney-General are thoroughly misplaced. The Kartripakkha did not even wait for a reasonable period before it framed its own scheme. Acquisition of land by private purchase often involves litigation and it is a time-consuming process. The Kartripakkha's own Uttara Block Statellite Town Project, undertaken in 1965 for acquisition of 950 acres of land is still, on its own admission, at the stage of final acquisition. To expect that within four years of the sanctioning of a layout plan the appellant will be able to achieve what the Kartripakkha with the coercive machinery of Ordinance No. 11 of 1982 has not been able to achieve within three decades is to ask for the moon. The Kartripakkha acted completely behind the back and without the knowledge of the appellant in changing the width and alignment of Uttara-Ranabhola Link Road and in forwarding its acquisition proposal on 16.9.87, without even caring to inquire how much progress the appellant had made and what expenses it had incurred in the meanwhile. Both the respondents are now claiming in their respective affidavits-in-opposition that the appellant did not fulfill the terms and conditions of approval, but there is little doubt that this allegation, besides being vague, is an afterthought aired for the first time to make out a case against the appellant. It is also now being alleged by the respondents that the appellant did not make any improvement as it claims to have made, and this allegation too is an afterthought, as respondent No. 2 did not even allege and never produced any materia to show that it framed its own scheme as the appellant failed to improve the land.

 55. There is nothing to show that the Ranabhola approach scheme for which lands were acquired in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 had been carried into execution before the appellant addressed its representation to the Chairman on 17.11.86. In fact LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 was still in its infancy at that stage. There is also nothing to show that while addressing its subsequent representations to the President on 2.10.89 and to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms on 30.10.89, the Kartripakkha's scheme in respect of LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 had already been carried into execution. LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 for 393 acres was started, according to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 1 (para 5) and according to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 2 (para 7), for the purpose of Uttara-Ranabhola road proper (and not its approach from the Uttara end) as well as for the Kartripakkha's housing project. This last LA case hit the appellant in real terms and before the scheme even got off to a start it moved the President this time so that the Kartripakkha may retrace its steps under section 52. The President himself did not take any action, but respondent No. 1 in pursuance of a noting from the President asked for a report from the Chairman. In his report dated 12.11.89 (Annexure-D) the Chairman did not state that its Uttara-Ranabhola approach road in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 or the road itself or the housing project in LA Case No.2 of 1987-88 had been carried into execution and, in fact, suggested some alternative including exclusion of the appellant's layout plan from its scheme and it was perfectly within his statutory power under section 52 of the said Act to do so. The Ministry of Works by Memo dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E), in fact, took a decision excluding the appellant's layout plan area, thus accepting the suggestion of the Kartripakkha and acting in exercise of its powers under section 191A Of the said Act which is as follows: 

 56. Respondent No. 1, the controlling Ministry of the Kartripakkha, after applying its mind, found that it was reasonable to exclude the appellant's land covered by the layout plan from the proposed acquisition and its decision, in view of the promises made to the appellant, was taken for ensuring that the activities of the Kartripakkha conform to the purposes of the Act. In Annexure-E, respondent No. 1 never indicated that the lands covered by the appellant's layout plan must be owned by the appellant. There was neither any absence of power nor any lack of legal cover in giving this decision. The order of respondent No. 1 dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E) was sabotaged by Annexure-H series on completely extraneous considerations. The appellant was not clamouring for compensation for acquisition of its land in the LA proceedings. It was only stating that it was given a promise to operate within a certain area which should be kept out of acquisition. Respondent No. 1 diverted the real issue by asking the appellant to produce its title deeds and mutation papers. This diversionary manoeuvre was aimed at establishing the proposition that either on the date of approval of the project (4.10.78) or on the date of the approval of the layout plan (27.2.83) the appellant must either own or possess the entire land of layout area or else its right is only limited to receipt of compensation for acquisition of land. What the Kartripakkha truly understood to be the appellant's main bone of contention (Annexure-D) and what respondent No. 1 rightly comprehended to be the main issue (Annexure-E) were now misdirected towards non-issues, namely, how much land the appellant owns and possesses now. And the entire Annexure-H series is a product of asking a wrong question and giving a wrong answer. 

 58. It is contended by the respondents that the appellant did not act to his detriment following any promise, it did not improve any land and it suffered no damages. I have already held that this allegation, made for the first time in the affidavits-in- opposition, is an afterthought, and deserves no serious consideration. The appellant's progress with its project was never inquired into by any of the respondents at any time. In any view of the matter, the following observations by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of MP Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1979 (SC) 651) is a complete answer to the respondents' submission: 

 59. It is accepted by the respondents that the appellant purchased some lands at least in its layout area and that is enough to say that it has altered its position as a result of the promise. The respondents' assertion that it had released from acquisition all the 65 bighas of land purchased by the appellant by Annexure-H2 is also palpably incorrect. The appellant purchased 32.86 acres of land, but by Annexure-H2 only 21.09 acres of land purchased by it have been released from acquisition. Its possession of another 150 bighas of land by contract of purchase has not been considered at all. 

 61. The respondents have neither placed any material nor any copy of a prior notice to the appellant to show that they had acted in an overriding public interest or that events that have subsequently transpired justify denial of an equity in favour of the appellant. There is nothing to show from the record, that a large part of the appellant's layout area was acquired in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 and the appellant merely stood by, sending only two representations to the Chairman. LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 was started for an approach to Uttara-Ranabhola Road and it presumably did not affect the appellant's layout area. But the LA Case alarmed the appellant which found that the proposed road alignment would spoil its 60 developed and 137 allotted plots. So it requested the Kartripakkha to retrace its steps under section 52 of the said Act. There is also nothing to show that in 1986 the Kartripakkha started construction of the link road to Ranabhola. It was only constructing the approach road from the Uttara end upon the Kartripakkha's acquired land. Annexure B precluded the appellant from questioning acquisition of land for the Kartripakkha for construction of bridges or culverts and their approaches to Ranabhola (not to Uttara). The width and alignment of the link road had already been settled and finalised between the appellant and the Kartripakkha by a protracted negotiation from 1978 to 1983. The appellant's layout plan contained a provision for 100 feet road. When the Kartripakkha changed the width and alignment of the link road without informing the appellant and behind its back, the appellant certainly had the legal right to object to such unilateral change disastrous to its project. It did so, timely and within the law. It was only when LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 was started that the link road proper with approach to Ranibhola and the housing project of the Kartripakkha was included in the 393 acres of land which included the appellant's layout area. It is nowhere the respondents case, not a word has been said anywhere, that the 300 feet link road has already been consumed within an unknown area of 300 bighas within the appellant's layout area. In fact, there is no material on record that the link road has at all been constructed. The respondents have not made out any case that within the 300 bighas of the appellant's layout area, provision has been made for public facilities like roads, bridges, schools, parks, etc. The Kartripakkha's layout plan has not been shown to us and we simply do not know what material benefit the residuary allottees of the appellant (as per Annexure-H2) will derive from the Kartripakkha's layout plan. The appellant's sanctioned layout plan contained a number of open spaces with provisions for playground, schools, park, internal roads (some as large as 40 feet wide), shopping centre, Community Centre, Commercial area, etc. How can it be said that the Kartripakkha was offering a better and more comprehensive service within easy access to the appellant's allottees within the layout area? The word 'public interest' is not a mere catchword. The Kartripakkha's scheme of better utility and convenience has to be shown to the Court which it has not. Besides, if all the Government orders (Annexure-E to H series) are not at all in accordance with law, then even Annexure-H2 falls, and the respondents are under no legal obligation to honour the minimum 'grace' granted to the appellant. All its 300 bighas are gone, including 21.09 acre so very graciously released from acquisition by Annexure-H2. The appellant had come to the writ jurisdiction for cancellation of Annexure-H series and the High Court Division refused to grant that prayer. How to say that not only Annexure-H series but also Annexure-E has no legal basis is, I think, a windfall received by the Government without disowning Annexure-E. Upon the facts disclosed in the affidavits-in-opposition I hold therefore that there was no overriding public interest, justified by subsequent events, to deny the equity in favour of the appellant.
